name: Centre Passage Core
description: A through-passage from front door to back, with the stair in it and rooms to either side. It is a circulation device, a climate device and a social device at once: it lets a visitor be received without entering a room, it draws air through the house on a summer afternoon, and it makes the facade symmetrical because the door is now genuinely in the middle.

rooms.note: Where the stair is separated from the passage rather than standing in it.

internal_rules.statement: Both ends of the passage have doors, and they are aligned. A passage closed at the back is a corridor and loses the reason the type exists.
Passage width 8 to 14 ft, and roughly one fifth to one quarter of the facade. Below 8 ft the stair cannot turn and the passage stops being a room.

Passage width 8 to 14 ft. Below 8 ft the stair cannot turn and the passage stops being a room. Stated as a rule of its own because the ratio rule above measures a different quantity -- the passage's share of the facade -- so this figure, which the same statement has always carried, was executable by nothing and could not be held against the room record it constrains.
Flanking rooms are equal or near-equal, and their windows align vertically with those above. The passage buys the symmetry and the symmetry has to be honoured.
The stair rises in the passage or in a hall opening off it, never through a room.
Where the plan is single-pile, the passage cross-ventilates the whole house. Filling in behind to make it double-pile buys area and loses the draft, and that trade should be made deliberately.

attaches_to.note: The single house is entered sideways off a piazza and has no through-passage; that is precisely its distinction.
Hall-less by design — the gallery is the circulation.

expansion_logic: Rear ell off one flanking room for service; or flanking dependencies joined by hyphens, which turns it into the five-part composition. Growth must respect the axis or the whole logic fails.
servicing_strategy: Paired gable-end stacks serving the flanking rooms; the passage itself is unheated and is the better for it.

style_variation.note: The canonical case, and the reason Georgian facades are symmetrical.
Passage often widens into an oval or apsidal stair hall at the rear, which is where Adamesque planning shows off.
Frequently becomes a side-hall plan when the gable turns to the street, which trades the cross-draft for a narrower lot.

sources: Glassie, Folk Housing in Middle Virginia
Waterman, The Dwellings of Colonial America
Upton, Architecture in the United States
